conflicts.name: Close-hauled
conflicts.text: Source says about 45 degrees close-hauled; the simulation's no-go half-width is about 36 degrees (Falua sails from about 35-40, 3.6 kn at 45), and the Rabelo needs 50 degrees.

conflicts.name: Leeboard
conflicts.text: Existing concept describes a board lowered to reduce slip in shallow water. The candidate (tábua de bolina) describes a lateral keel on one side, one per side on the muleta, for lateen-rigged flat-bottomed boats; it also adds dates (documented 1710, on other boats 1785) not in the existing concept. Possibly complementary rather than conflicting.

conflicts.name: Gust
conflicts.text: Method doc defines a gust as a sudden increase in wind. Fragateiro's gust_or_shift also includes changes in wind direction.

conflicts.name: Beating to windward
conflicts.text: Source gives 45–50 degrees to the wind while beating; the simulation has a no-go half-width of about 36 degrees (Falua nothing below about 35, Rabelo 50), so the figures differ by boat.

conflicts.name: Downwind sail setting rule
conflicts.text: Source says set sails at 90 degrees to the wind downwind; the simulation states no matching sail angle, and its sheet stop is 20 degrees.

conflicts.name: Bateiras (cargo boats)
conflicts.text: c278 'Bateiras' is described as cargo boats, while the candidate (Embarcações do Rio Tejo) describes bateiras as boats of Avieiro fishing communities that they also lived aboard; c349 describes a bateira as a small boat on the Lisbon run.

conflicts.name: Batel passenger limit
conflicts.text: The source gives two different passenger limits for the batel: 8 persons (paragraph 19) and 12 persons (paragraph 61).

conflicts.name: Scheduled service boat (barco da carreira)
conflicts.text: The sources give differing counts: one boat per week on the Lisbon run, 2-4 barcas per route, and 100 Abrantes boats in 1552.

conflicts.name: Estuary navigation (tidal reach)
conflicts.text: Candidates 1 and 2 give 20-30 km upstream of Lisbon as the limit of significant traffic, while candidate 37 says boats operated longest where the tide reaches (Sabugueiro, per candidates 11 and 12), a much longer reach; the tidal extent is stated differently.

conflicts.name: Square sail no-go angle
conflicts.text: Candidate 28 says the Rabelo's square sail cannot sail closer than about 50° to the wind, while candidate 29 says a square sail can be braced to 35°. Both describe the square-rig limit, so the numbers differ.

- Freire (page 4): The Prado paper mill had warehouses beside the steam quay on the east side of Barquinha town, so goods often arrived and left there.
- Freire (page 4): The Prado and Marianaia mills made writing, foolscap and wrapping papers from rags and wool, which required a warehouse at the Barquinha steam quay.
- Freire (page 4): Shipments of unspecified wool fabrics from Belgium and England, brought by steamboat, were stored in the Barquinha warehouse to be processed.
practices.name: Steam cargo and warehouse trade at Barquinha quay
practices.why: Steam cargo boats and warehouse trade at the Barquinha quay are not represented.

evidence: - Freire (page 4): Goods were moved from the warehouse onto ox carts and taken along the macadam district road no. 51 to the paper mills.
practices.name: Overland ox-cart transport to river ports
practices.why: Ox-cart haulage to paper mills is absent.

evidence: - Pedrosa (p. 14): Tartaranha fishermen supplied fish to Lisbon and acted as bar pilots assisting India ships, royal fleets and merchant ships.
- Pedrosa (p. 14): The first regulation for Lisbon bar pilotage admitted as pilots only those with ten years of continuous experience on offshore fishing boats.
- Pedrosa ([page 36]): Muleta crews also performed pilotage services.
- Pedrosa (page 37): The muleta served as the boat of the pilots of the Lisbon bar, in the main Portuguese port where sailors from everywhere passed.
practices.name: Tartaranha fishermen as bar pilots and fish suppliers
practices.why: Bar piloting of ocean-going ships is not offered; fishing grounds only.

evidence: - Pedrosa (page 17): During João IV's reign some Frenchmen sought to introduce a new model of tartaranha with a vessel also of a new type.

- Pedrosa ([page 17]): A king used the word tartana (vessel) together with tartaranha (net) in a letter, after deep-sea line-and-hook fishermen had opposed a French fishing proposal and the king refused it.
- Pedrosa ([page 17]): Two Frenchmen again asked to introduce the new tartaranha net and vessel; the king passed the request to Lisbon's city senate, which advised against it and the king refused.
- Pedrosa ([page 17]): The senate argued French tartanas resembled the launches of Moorish corsairs who raided the coast, so fishermen might mistake them and confront them by accident.
- Pedrosa ([page 17]): Estevam da Luz asked leave to build four large vessels at his own expense to fish far out at sea; the king granted a four-year exclusive licence.
- Pedrosa ([page 17-18]): The Espírito Santo brotherhood, representing deep-sea fishermen, again opposed the petition, but the senate called the invention very useful and favoured it.
practices.name: French proposals to introduce the tartana in Portugal
practices.why: Historical proposals to introduce the tartana are not a playable activity.

evidence: - Pedrosa ([page 18]): Spanish author Veitia Linage described tartanas as lateen-sailed Levantine-crewed vessels suited to fishing at sea, some sent to the Indies; foreign sailors were needed for the sails.
- Pedrosa ([page 18]): The tartana had lateen sails for navigating and extra sails for trawl fishing, which required foreign (French) sailors.
- Pedrosa (16. As Velas e a Rede): Duhamel Du Monceau said the French tartana could trawl with four to ten sails, though known images show fewer.
practices.name: Tartana rigging and foreign crews
practices.why: Tartana rigging and foreign crews are not represented in the game.

evidence: - Pedrosa ([page 18]): The oldest known illustration of the French fishing tartana appears in an album by Jean Jouve of Marseilles.

- Pedrosa ([page 18, section 10]): The earliest illustration of the muleta, not yet mentioned by Portuguese authors, appears in Gueroult du Pas's album published in Paris, which also shows the tartana for fishing off Provence and Italy.
- Pedrosa ([page 18]): Figure 2 shows three tartanas: one with a single mast and lateen sail, one with an extra triangular sail on a pole, one fully rigged for beam trawling.

- Pedrosa ([page 18-20]): The muleta is shown under way without trawl rigging, with a forward-leaning mast, lateen sail, forward boom with a square sail, raised inward-curving ends and a leeboard on each quarter.
- Pedrosa ([page 28]): The tartana, used for fishing and cargo, is documented at Sanlúcar de Barrameda since the 18th century; a c.1910-1920 photo shows a muleta-like one-mast lateen rig.
practices.name: Early illustrations of tartana and muleta
practices.why: Early illustrations are documentary, not a playable activity.

evidence: - Pedrosa ([page 20]): This is the first documentation of the leeboard in Portugal; it appears on other vessels only later, in the Caderno de todos os barcos do Tejo.

- Pedrosa ([page 20]): The muleta has three features never seen on French fishing tartanas: inward-curving bow and stern, forward-leaning mast, and leeboard. The 1710 album shows leeboards only on Atlantic boats.

- Pedrosa ([page 20]): The leeboard reduces leeward drift and prevents capsizing; it is needed only on flat or nearly flat-bottomed lateen-rigged boats, not on round-rigged ones, and is lowered on one side.
- Pedrosa ([page 20]): Two theories exist on the leeboard's origin in Europe; one holds it is Chinese and reached Holland in the late 16th century.
- Pedrosa ([page 21]): The muleta's leeboard took several different shapes, while the Dutch yacht (jachten) sailing the Indian Ocean had a very large one.

- Pedrosa ([page 21]): The muleta used its leeward leeboard while sailing to reduce leeway, one board on each side; Portuguese authors name it variously (tábua de bolina, pau de borda, pá de borda, esparrela de deriva, tábua de abatimento).
practices.name: Leeboard of the muleta and its origins
practices.why: Leeboard origins are history; the game offers no equivalent activity.

evidence: - Pedrosa ([page 23]): The muleta fished with the tartaranha net in the Tagus and Sado estuaries and at sea between Cabo da Roca and Setúbal.
- Embarcações do Rio Tejo (2.2): Muletas are registered at south-bank ports such as Barreiro and Seixal but fish in the Embocadura waters called Entre-Cabos.
- Pedrosa ([page 5]): The tartaranha targeted flatfish living on sand (azevias, linguados, solhas) but also caught other species from seabed to surface.
practices.name: Muleta fishing grounds with tartaranha net
practices.why: Muleta drifts sideways dragging net at Seixal, Barra and Cascais grounds.

evidence: - Pedrosa ([page 29]): Muletas and rascas ventured beyond the bar, sometimes many miles out, seeking cargo from abundant ocean fisheries.
- barcos do tejo ([page 3]): The rasca sails out over the bar to load figs at Algarve ports.
practices.name: Muletas and rascas trading beyond the bar
practices.why: Muleta at sea is served by canoa, but no cargo-seeking beyond the bar.

evidence: - Pedrosa ([page 29]): Muletas did coastal trading to the Algarve, bringing its products to the Tagus or exchanging them at Moroccan ports.
practices.name: Muleta coastal trade to Algarve and Morocco
practices.why: No coastal trade routes to the Algarve or Morocco.

evidence: - Pedrosa ([pages 29-30]): A muleta could be rigged as a yacht (iate) with two or three masts for some commercial commission.
- barcos do tejo ([page 3]): The moleta, used in fishing, is also rigged as a hiate to carry out some commercial commission.
practices.name: Muleta rigged as iate
practices.why: No multi-masted iate rig option for the muleta.

evidence: - Pedrosa ([page 30]): Furling the sail: crew climbed the yard, first reducing sail area with brails, then rolling the cloth by hand and securing it.
practices.name: Furling the muleta sail
practices.why: Furling by climbing the yard and brailing is not modelled.

evidence: - Pedrosa ([page 32]): Rebelo says muletas paid out cable so the net reached the bottom, hauls lasted hours and the net was hauled by hand; the author doubts this.
- Pedrosa ([page 32]): Comparable boats used hoisting gear for nets: the lancha poveira had a windlass, and Dutch fishing ships show nets rigged to cables going to the masthead.
practices.name: Hauling the tartaranha net
practices.why: Net dragging is covered, but not paying out cable or hauling by hand.

evidence: - Pedrosa ([page 32]): The author corrects other writers: the beach-hauled net described at Costa de Caparica is the xávega, not the tartaranha net.
practices.name: Xávega beach-hauled net at Costa de Caparica
practices.why: Beach-hauled xávega net fishing is not offered.

evidence: - Pedrosa ([page 36]): A 1730 description of Lisbon reports a huge quantity of fish unloaded by caravelles and muletes.
practices.name: Fish landing at Lisbon by muletas
practices.why: Bringing fish home is included, but not landing catches at Lisbon.

evidence: - Pedrosa ([page 36]): Each cod-fishing ship carried several small boats that left at dawn daily from the fishing ground and returned at dusk with the catch.
- Pedrosa ([page 36]): Around 1875 the small boats carried by cod ships became dories; before that they were larger and heavier.
practices.name: Cod ships' small boats
practices.why: Doris fishing from cod ships is not represented.

evidence: - Embarcações do Rio Tejo (Embarcações do Médio Tejo): Boats of the Middle Tagus worked river fishing, transport and crossings between Vila Velha de Rodão and Constância, using oars.
- Embarcações do Rio Tejo (Embarcações do Baixo Tejo): Lower Tagus boats did river fishing, transport and crossings between Constância and Santarém.
- Embarcações do Rio Tejo (Embarcações do Baixo Tejo): Avieira boats were used for river fishing and as dwellings between Santarém and Sacavém.
- Embarcações do Rio Tejo (Embarcações do Baixo Tejo): Lower Tagus boats are listed with types such as canoa, bateira, catrafuço, culé, barco do tráfego and varino, with dimensions given.
- Embarcações do Rio Tejo (Embarcações do Estuário - Mouchões): Around Vila Franca de Xira, small boats did river fishing, carried fish and small goods, and ferried people.

practices.name: Boat types and uses by Tagus section

evidence: - Embarcações do Rio Tejo (Mar da Palha (1)): Boats carried passengers between Cacilhas, Almada and Lisbon.
practices.name: Bote passenger service Cacilhas-Almada-Lisboa
practices.why: Passengers across the river between Lisbon and Almada, as catraios did.

evidence: - Embarcações do Rio Tejo (Mar da Palha (1)): Larger keel boats carried people and cargo from Cacilhas to Ribatejo ports and the estuary's south bank.
practices.name: Keel boats carrying people and cargo from Cacilhas
practices.why: Cargo from the south bank to Lisbon; larger boats carry freight.

evidence: - Embarcações do Rio Tejo (Mar da Palha (4)): The bote of the tapa-esteiros fishing art fished with support from the canoa das redes.
practices.name: Tapa-esteiros fishing in Mar da Palha
practices.why: Tapa-esteiros fishing with a supporting canoa das redes is not offered.

evidence: - Embarcações do Rio Tejo (2.2): Avieiros, from Praia da Vieira, fished almost exclusively in the river, living aboard bateiras or in stilt-house villages they created.
practices.name: Avieiros fishing and living aboard bateiras
practices.why: Avieiro river fishing and living aboard bateiras are not modelled.

evidence: - Embarcações do Rio Tejo (2.2): In the Mouchões, some Avieiros remain, but the main activity is traffic and freight transport, partly in boats native to Vila Franca de Xira.
practices.name: Avieiros and freight traffic in the Mouchões
practices.why: Freight near Vila Franca exists, but not Mouchões or native boats.

evidence: - Embarcações do Rio Tejo (2.2): Foz and Embocadura are devoted to sea fishing, with fishermen from all over Portugal, including Galicians.
- Embarcações do Rio Tejo (2.2): Fishing boats there are either keeled with transom stern, suggesting southern origin, or double-ended flat-bottomed, typical of the Aveiro lagoon.
practices.name: Sea fishing at Foz and Embocadura
practices.why: Fishing grounds at the river mouth exist, but with Muleta drift-netting, not Galician fishermen.

evidence: - barcos do tejo ([page 3]): Most of these boats came from the Barreiro and Seixal shipyards, whose residents also commonly formed their crews; Trafaria residents supplied most fishing crews.
practices.name: Crews and shipyards of Barreiro, Seixal and Trafaria
practices.why: Shipyard building and crew origins are not playable; only sailing the boats.

evidence: - barcos do tejo ([page 3]): The largest boats with the most crew came from shipyards at Esposende, Figueira, Porto and other northern coastal towns.
practices.name: Large boats built in northern coastal shipyards
practices.why: Northern shipyards and large-crew boats are not represented in any activity.

evidence: - barcos do tejo (Figura 11): A figure caption shows a boat being hauled by towing from the riverbank while passing the Cachão do Cabril rapids.
practices.name: Towing boats from the bank at Cachão do Cabril
practices.why: No towing from the bank or rapids passage in the game.

evidence: - Cacilheiros no Rio Tejo (Cacilheiros section): From early times botes, catraios and faluas linked Lisbon with Montijo, formerly Aldeia Galega or Aldegalega.
- Barcos Tradicionais do Tejo e  (Pintura Decorativa): Faluas formed a fairly regular network carrying passengers; a children's rhyme about a falua from Belém survives.
practices.name: Boat service Lisbon to Montijo (Aldeia Galega)
practices.why: Lisbon–south bank crossings exist, but not Montijo or Aldeia Galega specifically.

evidence: - Cacilheiros no Rio Tejo (Cacilheiros section): Some ferries also carried cars.
- Cacilheiros no Rio Tejo (photo captions): A ferry-boat crossed between Cacilhas and Cais do Sodré and between Porto Brandão and Belém, carrying cars and donkey-drawn vegetable carts.
- Cacilheiros no Rio Tejo (photo captions): Carlos Alberto Figueiredo worked for several years on the ferry Eborense.
practices.name: Car-carrying ferries
practices.why: No car-carrying ferries; transport covers passengers and cargo by sail only.

evidence: - Barcos Tradicionais do Tejo e  (Tipologias): Cangueiros hauled heavy cargo including building materials, sand, stone and pine to fuel Lisbon's bread ovens.
practices.name: Cangueiros hauling heavy cargo to Lisbon
practices.why: Cargo from south bank to Lisbon, but not specific heavy materials or cangueiro boats.

evidence: - Barcos Tradicionais do Tejo e  (Pintura Decorativa): Varinos, faluas and fragatas were the most decorated boats, with floral motifs and decorated lettering; each painter's style identified the boat's shipyard.
- Barcos Tradicionais do Tejo e  (Pintura Decorativa): The colour sequence painted on the calcês, the upper mast, was mandatory in the register and identified a boat's origin and ownership.

- Barcos Tradicionais do Tejo e  (Pintura Decorativa): Painting used bright red, blue, green, yellow and white chosen by painter or owner, without symbolism; pigment paints were later replaced by industrial paints.

- Barcos Tradicionais do Tejo e  (Pintura Decorativa): Painters worked directly on the surface without preliminary drawing, except for symmetry, applying one colour at a time to all elements, with no precision instruments.
practices.name: Decorative painting of Tagus boats
practices.why: Boat decoration and painting is not a game activity.

evidence: - Pedrosa ([page 4]): Caravels from Galicia sailed to Cabo Branco to fish sharks and mullets, which were dried in the sun like cod from Newfoundland.
practices.name: Galician caravels fishing at Cabo Branco
practices.why: No ocean fishing voyage to Cabo Branco; fishing grounds are near Portugal.

evidence: - Pedrosa ([page 6]): Despite the ban, each Lent some tartaranhas in the Tagus estuary fished azevias and linguados to supply the king in Madrid.
- Pedrosa ([page 6]): Lisbon's câmara stated the yearly fishing of azevias and linguados for His Majesty's Lenten meals.
practices.name: Lenten flatfish fishing for the king despite tartaranha ban
practices.why: Tagus estuary fishing exists, but not Lenten ban, tartaranhas or royal supply.

evidence: - jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT ([page 2]): In the early 15th century Almada and Ribatejo (Montijo) linked Lisbon with the south, with Coina also important; fish from Setúbal and Arrábida came through them.

- jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT ([page 2]): People and goods from the Alentejo, mainly firewood from Montijo and Canha districts for Lisbon fuel, came via Ribatejo; some fish went on to Santarém and upriver ports.
- jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT ([page 2]): Salt, fish (dried, salted, smoked or fresh) and cloth were the main goods carried upriver from Lisbon to Santarém, Abrantes and Punhete.
- jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT ([page 2]): Goods sent downriver to Lisbon included timber, olive oil, wine, hides, honey, wax, iron and river fish (shad, azevias, lampreys).

- jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT ([page 2]): Santarém was the most important middle Tagus port, followed by Abrantes and Punhete; the author defines the middle Tagus as Abrantes to Sabugueiro, where tide begins.
practices.name: 15th-century trade between Lisbon, the south bank and upriver
practices.why: South bank to Lisbon cargo routes exist; Coina and Santarém links are absent.

evidence: - jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT ([page 2]): The king travelled by boat between the Royal Palace of Almeirim and Lisbon (Paço de Xabregas or Paço da Ribeira).
- BOOK Territorios da Lisboa Med (page 230): As King Manuel favoured stays at the Almeirim palace, royal and court journeys up the Tagus became frequent, linked to hunting and leisure.
- BOOK Territorios da Lisboa Med (note 29): The king travelled by boat from the royal palace at Almeirim to Lisbon (Paço de Xabregas or Paço da Ribeira), using the river as transport.
- BOOK Territorios da Lisboa Med (note 30): The river served as a natural road for the court, which was drawn to Almeirim by hunting, fertile fields, pleasant climate and views.
practices.name: Royal boat travel Almeirim-Lisbon
practices.why: No royal travel or Almeirim route; upriver routes stop at Abrantes.

evidence: - jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT ([page 2]): Large quantities of melons from the Santarém and Abrantes lezírias were carried to Lisbon as a new item; wine arrived by river, named after loading ports.
- jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT ([page 2]): Four barcas came from Muge to Lisbon two to three times a week, and likewise from Azambuja.
practices.name: 16th-century produce and wine shipped to Lisbon
practices.why: Long lezíria-to-Lisbon haul exists, but not melons, wine or Santarém ports.

evidence: - jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT ([page 2]): Three barcas and batéis came from Vila Nova da Rainha to Lisbon two to three times a week.
- jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT ([page 2]): Four barcas came from Benavente to Lisbon three to four times a week.
- jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT ([page 2]): Brandão gives data only for the lower Tagus, probably because middle and upper river voyages were more irregular owing to various constraints.
- jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT (page start): Table of boats serving Lisbon by port lists Sacavém, Alhandra and Lisbon and surroundings, totalling 1490 boats and batéis serving Lisbon.
- jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT (page start): Boats carried firewood, wheat and straw, plus people and other goods, on weekly runs.
practices.name: Boats serving Lisbon from Tagus ports in 16th century
practices.why: Upriver-to-Lisbon transport exists, but not Vila Nova da Rainha or scheduled service.

evidence: - jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT (page 160): In the mid-19th century Portuguese boats, mostly from Rossio de Abrantes, Pego and Alvega, carried Alcántara ore to Lisbon in convoys of at least ten boats so crews could help each other with towing at rapids.
- jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT (page 16): Until the railway arrived, the Spanish town of Alcantara exported its ores down the Tagus to Lisbon.
- jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT ([page 17] Summary): Before railways, the Spanish town of Alcantara exported its ore down the Tagus via Lisbon.
practices.name: Alcántara ore convoys to Lisbon
practices.why: No ore convoys or Alcántara rapids route in the game.

evidence: - jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT (page 161): Larger boats could not navigate in dry season, even at Abrantes; in summer timber and cork went by raft to Salvaterra de Magos or Valada, then by boat to Lisbon.
- jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT ([page 5]): Timber rafts went from Praia do Ribatejo to Valada or Salvaterra until 1950.
- jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT (page 9, p.180): Timber from the Zêzere basin reached the Tagus by floating or ox carts, then was loaded onto rafts or boats; the area drove river transport.
- jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT (page 184): Timber was taken from the riverbed at a large sandbank below the confluence, loaded on rafts to Valada or Salvaterra, then carried by boat to Lisbon.
- jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT (page 13, Abrantes-Rossio): Timber from areas north of the Tagus was the main export by volume from Abrantes, but mostly travelled on rafts rather than boats.

- jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT ([page 14] Constância and Praia do Ribatejo): Praia do Ribatejo developed as a secondary port specialised in exporting timber, sent down the Tejo by boats and especially rafts, mainly in summer.
practices.name: Dry-season rafting of timber and cork
practices.why: Timber and cork rafting is not offered; no raft boat.

evidence: - jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT ([page 4]): Boatmen leaving upriver ports moved their boats to work on the lower Tagus; others sold boats and became lorry operators, merchants or retirees.
- jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT ([page 4]): Many mariners from Vila Nova da Barquinha and Moita took jobs at the railway company in Entroncamento, leaving the river.
- jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT ([page 5]): In the 1930s seamen of Barquinha and Moita moved to the railway; C.P. bought some boats at Vila Nova da Barquinha, and José da Silva bought one there.
- jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT (page 16): Boatmen's fates differed: some moved to the estuary with their boats, some turned to trade or farming at home, some drive lorries.
practices.name: Boatmen leaving upriver ports
practices.why: Boatmen's career shifts are not a playable activity.

evidence: - jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT ([page 5]): José da Silva, a former boat businessman, had a 60 t boat built at Constância by the Zêzere in 1945 and sold it to Alcochete two years before the interview.

- jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT ([page 5]): His last freight of timber from Constância to Lisbon was 23 years earlier; afterwards he carried fertilisers and sulphates from CUF Barreiro to Santarém for onward rail transport.

- jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT ([page 5]): He later worked the Lisbon markets, carrying wine from Sabugueiro, Cartaxo, Salvaterra and Vala do Carregado to Lisbon and Cacilhas (Ginjal); he sold his boat in 1958 and retired.
practices.name: José da Silva's boat business at Constância
practices.why: Boat business and construction at Constância are not represented.

evidence: - jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT ([page 8]): Heath scrub on the poor sandy charneca was kept productive for firewood and charcoal, with the king caring for it as the most profitable use for the nation.
- jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT ([page 8]): In the 19th century other products became more profitable than scrub, and vineyards gradually replaced it in the Poceirão-Taipadas-Canha area.

- jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT ([page 8]): When transporting firewood stopped paying, it was made into charcoal; charcoal-burning areas on the periphery moved closer to the river and stopped exporting firewood to Lisbon.
- jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT ([page 8]): Distant areas with good sea access supplied charcoal to Lisbon: the coast from Feira to Buarcos, the Algarve and the Alentejo coast.
practices.name: Charneca scrub, firewood and charcoal
practices.why: Land-based scrub, firewood and charcoal production has no game equivalent.

evidence: - jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT ([page 8]): Lime kilns on the north side, where suitable limestone exists, sent lime to Lisbon through the nearest river ports.
- jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT ([page 8]): Lime kilns at Alenquer, Ota, Atouguia das Cabras and Portela shipped lime to Lisbon via the port of Vila Nova da Rainha.
- jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT ([page 8]): Lime from Aveiras went out through Virtudes; from Pontével and Cartaxo through Vale da Pedra; from Almoster through Porto de Muge.
practices.name: Lime shipment to Lisbon via river ports
practices.why: Generic cargo transport exists, but no lime or north-bank port route.

evidence: - jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT (page 9, p.180): When wine came from too far and quality could not cover freight, it was turned into brandy to cut mass and cargo cost.
practices.name: Brandy distilling to cut freight cost
practices.why: Brandy distilling is a land economic practice, not in the game.

evidence: - jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT (page 183): Timber received first treatment at the felling site: felled trees were cleaned and trunks sorted by size, reducing mass and transport cost before shipping.
- jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT (pages 183-184): Trunks were carried to the Tagus by ox carts, or floated down the Zêzere, then embarked at river points for Lisbon.

- jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT ([page 14] Constância and Praia do Ribatejo): Timber from the north floated down the Zêzere and was collected on a beach just downstream of the confluence with the Tejo.
practices.name: Timber felling and transport to Tagus
practices.why: Timber felling and sorting are not playable.

evidence: - jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT (page 187): Most cork reached Rossio de Abrantes by rail, then went by boat, more rarely by raft, to the Lisbon area.

- jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT (page 12 (start)): Cork from Alto Alentejo reached Rossio de Abrantes by rail from Ponte de Sor or on mule carts, often owned by Algarvians who came up for the cork harvest.
- jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT (page 12): Cork was taken to riverside warehouses in summer and shipped by boat in winter; summer rafts, mainly used for timber, carried much less cork. It left raw.
practices.name: Cork shipping from Rossio de Abrantes
practices.why: Upriver Abrantes route exists, but no cork cargo or Rossio-to-Lisbon run.

evidence: - jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT (page 12 (189)): Rossio was the upper limit for boats of 50-70 t, with upstream navigation much harder, so it became an intense wholesale centre supplying the Alentejo and Beira Baixa muleteers.
- jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT (page 12 (189)): Boats returning upriver from Lisbon carried salt, salted fish, other food and manufactures to Rossio; wine came mainly from Almeirim and Chamusca.

- jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT (page 12 (189-190)): Rossio redistributed goods to local trade and to muleteers from the Alentejo and Beira, who brought back olive oil, potatoes, cheese and other goods.
- jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT (page 12 (190)): The railway reduced and nearly ended the flow of muleteers from the Beiras and Alentejo, though Rossio kept its wholesale role.
- jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT (page 13, start of excerpt): Many wholesalers of groceries, wine and salt left Rossio; new truck-based wholesalers set up along main roads instead of at the quay.
- jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT (page 16, p.202): Rossio de Abrantes became a leading wholesale grocery centre thanks to its port, which outlasted the railway; road traffic now replaces it.
practices.name: Rossio de Abrantes wholesale and redistribution
practices.why: Wholesale and redistribution trade at Rossio is not represented.

evidence: - jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT (page 13, start of excerpt): Liquid fuel was carried by barge from Lisbon to Abrantes; at the Rossio quay, pumps and piping moved it from boats into depots beside the railway station.
practices.name: Fuel barges to Rossio quay
practices.why: No fuel barges or pumping at Abrantes quay.

evidence: - jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT (page 13, Abrantes-Rossio): Boats carried goods to Lisbon, mostly from the Alentejo: wheat before the railway, then cork as its trade grew.
practices.name: Boat freight from Rossio to Lisbon
practices.why: Long cargo haul to Lisbon exists, but not Rossio, wheat or cork.

evidence: - jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT ([page 14] Valada): Dikes were built to protect Valada from floods; the present embankment is recent but probably follows earlier ones.
practices.name: Valada flood dikes
practices.why: Flood dike building is not a game activity.

evidence: - jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT ([page 15] Résumé): In the Middle Ages the port of Santarém kept direct maritime links with North Africa and central Europe.

practices.name: Medieval Santarém maritime links
practices.why: Medieval maritime trade with North Africa and Europe is absent.

evidence: - jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT ([page 15] Résumé): Abrantes organised foreign trade for much of the Beira and Upper Alentejo.
practices.name: Abrantes foreign trade organisation
practices.why: Organising foreign trade is not a sailing activity in the game.

evidence: - jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT ([page 15] Résumé): Goods carried upriver on the Tagus were mainly food, especially salt and fish, and manufactured products.
- jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT ([page 17] Summary): Salt, fish and manufactured goods were carried up the Tagus; agricultural, livestock and forest products went downstream to Lisbon.

practices.why: Cargo routes go up and down the Tagus, but not upriver salt and fish.

evidence: - jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT (page 16): The railway company offered boatmen jobs and advantages, sometimes buying their boats.

- jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT ([page 17] Summary): Railways ended all navigation upstream of Abrantes and nearly killed Vila Nova da Barquinha's port; the railway company gave boat owners jobs and advantages, sometimes buying their boats.
practices.name: Railway company hiring boatmen and buying boats
practices.why: Railway company employment and boat purchases are economic history; no game activity covers it.

evidence: - jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT (page 16, p.201): Timber from the western coast reached Lisbon by sea, lowering transport costs.

- jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT ([page 17] Summary): Timber from distant regions reached Lisbon by coastal shipping from the western coast, or by log-floating on the Zêzere, rafts on the Tagus, then barges from the tidal limit.
practices.name: Western coast timber reaching Lisbon by sea
practices.why: No timber cargo carried by barge or raft to Lisbon exists in the game.

evidence: - BOOK Territorios da Lisboa Med (page 228, note 16): Crews struggled upriver, fighting winter current and summer sandbanks, pushing boats with poles or towing them from the bank, often running aground.
practices.name: Upriver crews poling and towing barcos de água acima
practices.why: Upper Tagus routes exist, but no poling or towing against current.

evidence: - BOOK Territorios da Lisboa Med (page 229): At rent-collection time barcas called more intensely at customary places, preferably Porto de Muge, so tenant farmers could meet their obligations.
practices.name: Barcas calling at Porto de Muge at rent time
practices.why: Transport covers river passage, but not Porto de Muge or rent-time calls.

evidence: - BOOK Territorios da Lisboa Med (page 229): Timber floated down the river to the tercenas (arsenals) in Lisboa, a massive presence on the Lower Tejo.
- BOOK Territorios da Lisboa Med (footnote 22): The charters of Povos and Vila Franca de Xira set a payment on timber coming down the river, suggesting river transport of wood.
practices.name: Timber floated and shipped to Lisbon
practices.why: Long haul downriver to Lisbon exists, but not floated timber or tercenas.

evidence: - BOOK Territorios da Lisboa Med (footnote 24): Santarém region supplied Lisbon with cereals, and its royal woodlands were exploited to supply arsenals and construction in Lisbon.
practices.name: Santarém region supplying Lisbon with cereals and timber
practices.why: Cargo to Lisbon exists, but not Santarém cereals, timber or woodland exploitation.

evidence: - BOOK Territorios da Lisboa Med (page 230 and footnote 25): The Tagus served as a busy liquid highway, with goods moving between Lisbon and Santarém in both directions and routes up, down and across.

- BOOK Territorios da Lisboa Med ([page 240] conclusion): Various vessels sailed between Lisbon and Santarém, forming a road of many purposes; both cities shared the medieval Tagus, linked to royal power.
practices.name: Medieval Tagus as busy river highway
practices.why: Tagus transport routes exist, but not the Lisbon-Santarém two-way medieval trade.

evidence: - BOOK Territorios da Lisboa Med (page 231, note 33): Riverside villagers shared the water, managing fresh water through ditches, openings, canals and channels while working the fields along the Tagus.
practices.name: Riverside villagers managing fresh water
practices.why: Village freshwater management through ditches and canals is not represented.

evidence: - BOOK Territorios da Lisboa Med (page 231): River fishermen lived from the waters, facing strong currents and sometimes tragedy.
- BOOK Territorios da Lisboa Med (note 35): A document confirming privileges of Vila Franca de Xira fishermen notes they have boats to go fishing and earn their food.

- BOOK Territorios da Lisboa Med (page 233): Fishermen left riverside ports for river fishing, using techniques and net types suited to the size and quality of the fish, refined over many generations.
- BOOK Territorios da Lisboa Med (page 233, note 43): Shad from the Tagus was caught with the boats of Prince Henry and those of Ceuta, and carried to Ceuta to be salted or sold.

- BOOK Territorios da Lisboa Med ([page 239] footnote 91): The king's privilege charter to Vila Franca de Xira fishermen set penalties for misusing fishermen's batéis; half of the fines went to the town's quay works.
practices.name: Medieval Tagus river fishing
practices.why: Fishing exists, but with a Muleta off Seixal, not river bateis or avargas.

evidence: - BOOK Territorios da Lisboa Med (p. 234): Beyond professional fishing, people could fish on their own from the riverbank using the available resources.
- BOOK Territorios da Lisboa Med (p. 234, note 54): Angling with rods or lines was done at river beaches, channels, caneiras and fishing spots not owned by lords or the crown.
- BOOK Territorios da Lisboa Med (p. 234): A skilled fisherman might catch fish by hand.
practices.name: Riverbank and angling fishing on the Tagus
practices.why: Bank and angling fishing from shore is not offered; fishing is boat-based.

evidence: - BOOK Territorios da Lisboa Med ([page 236]): Fishing on the Tagus followed the daily rhythm of local people, who caught fish either to sell or for their own consumption, with different implications.
- BOOK Territorios da Lisboa Med ([page 236]): Two main markets absorbed the Tagus catch: Santarém, where river fish competed with sea fish, and Lisbon, a larger but more contested market.
- BOOK Territorios da Lisboa Med ([page 236] footnote 61): Sea fish, some caught at the Tagus mouth, reached Santarém carried upriver by boat, competing with local river fish.
- BOOK Territorios da Lisboa Med (footnote 57): Fishers of Vila Franca de Xira held confirmed privileges to sell their fish, both fresh and salted and cured at home.
- BOOK Territorios da Lisboa Med (footnote 61): Some people bought large amounts of fish, loading and shipping it by sea out of the kingdom, and by water from Lisbon to Santarém and elsewhere.

- BOOK Territorios da Lisboa Med (footnote 62): After the bells for terce mass, Lisbon's Ribeira came alive: sea fishers unloaded boats, resellers bought freely, and loading and unloading went on all day.
practices.name: Tagus fish markets and trade
practices.why: Fishing exists, but no selling at markets or Santarém and Lisbon trade.

evidence: - BOOK Territorios da Lisboa Med (footnote 63): King D. João I's household was supplied with large quantities of fresh and dried fish and shellfish by royal buyer Afonso Anes over twelve years.
- BOOK Territorios da Lisboa Med (note 68): King Afonso V, staying at Santarém, had sea fish and shellfish at his table, brought to Santarém by land and river.
- BOOK Territorios da Lisboa Med (note 69): Oysters were bought cheaply for the king's table, probably eaten raw though they could be cooked.
practices.name: Supplying the royal household with fish
practices.why: Royal household fish supply and buyers are not represented.

evidence: - BOOK Territorios da Lisboa Med (note 73): Dead young shad were sold in baskets over the hills like sardines, and large quantities were wasted by being thrown into the water.
practices.name: Wasteful sale of young shad
practices.why: Wasteful sale of young shad has no game equivalent.

evidence: - moliceiro-Matriz PCI (Contexto tipológico): Moliceiro boats are built of pine (pinho manso and bravo) by traditional shipwrights, fitted to navigating the Ria de Aveiro and to its original economic use.
- moliceiro-Matriz PCI (Caracterização síntese): The moliceiro has a flat bottom for shallow lagoon waters and low sides so the rakes full of moliço can be pulled aboard easily.
- moliceiro-Matriz PCI (Caracterização síntese): Construction know-how, tools and skills are passed from masters to apprentices over decades, not only within families.
- moliceiro-Matriz PCI (Caracterização síntese): Masters build the whole boat using the pau-de-pontos, a handmade wooden rod serving as a ruler that only experienced builders can interpret.
- moliceiro-Matriz PCI (Contexto temporal): Building, repair work (amanhações) and panel painting occur year-round, whenever owners place new orders.
- moliceiro-Matriz PCI ([page 2]): The moliceiro is described as a boat about 15 m long with 5 tonnes capacity, essential for gathering moliço and tied to a distinctive naval carpentry art.
practices.name: Moliceiro construction
practices.why: Boat construction and materials are not playable.

evidence: - moliceiro-Matriz PCI (Caracterização síntese): Boats were used to gather moliço, aquatic plants from the lagoon bed, which served as fertilizer for farmland; this was a major regional economic activity.
- moliceiro-Matriz PCI (A origem do Barco Moliceiro): The boat was born for gathering moliço, a vital complement to subsistence farming, and worked across the whole lagoon.
- moliceiro-Matriz PCI (A Apanha do Moliço): Farmers began gathering moliço (aquatic plants) from the ria to fertilize sandy soils beside it, especially from the 18th/19th centuries.
- moliceiro-Matriz PCI (A Apanha do Moliço): Moliço gathering was first done by farmers, then grew into an independent profession, the moliceiro, supplying farmers as agriculture expanded.
- moliceiro-Matriz PCI (A Apanha do Moliço): Until the mid-1960s moliço gathering was a main source of wealth and employment for regional families.
- moliceiro-Matriz PCI (part 9, opening paragraph): The moliceiro was a main tool of the moliço-gathering trade; as more people worked in it, more boats were built and sailed on the Ria.
practices.name: Moliço gathering with moliceiros
practices.why: Gathering floating moliço with the Moliceiro in the Ria de Aveiro.

evidence: - moliceiro-Matriz PCI (Caracterização síntese): Each moliceiro carries decorated panels, each with a drawing and caption read together; no two panels repeat, and themes may be humorous, satirical, religious or other.

- moliceiro-Matriz PCI (page 3, Os painéis de moliceiros): No moliceiro is considered finished until decorated; its four painted panels (two bow, two stern) make it famed as the most beautiful boat of the Ria.
- moliceiro-Matriz PCI (page 3, Os painéis de moliceiros): The panels are naïf painting with vivid colour, bold outlines, everyday themes and humorous captions; borders frame the central scene.

- moliceiro-Matriz PCI (painel): Painters decorate the central panel with a drawing on themes such as religion, profession, history, homeland or love, usually from their own imagination, with little input from the owner or master.
- moliceiro-Matriz PCI (painel): Each panel drawing comes with a caption painted on a white or pink band below the frieze, between the frieze and the main motif.
- moliceiro-Matriz PCI (painel): Moliceiro panels almost always use pure primary colours: yellow, green, blue, red, white and black.
practices.name: Moliceiro panel painting
practices.why: Panel painting and decoration are not offered as activities.

evidence: - moliceiro-Matriz PCI (page 3, Métodos de propulsão): Poling (andar à vara): crew push a pine pole against the lagoon bed from bow towards stern when windless or near quays and banks.
- moliceiro-Matriz PCI (page 3, Métodos de propulsão): Towing (andar à sirga): a crew member walks the bank pulling the boat by rope in narrow channels or against tide or wind.
- moliceiro-Matriz PCI (page 3, Métodos de propulsão): Alternative towing rig: the sirga is fixed to the xarolo and passed through the bow block, so two crew can work the rudder from anywhere.
- moliceiro-Matriz PCI (page 3, Métodos de propulsão): Sailing (andar à vela) is the usual propulsion; crew use the bolinão rope and bow block to tension the sail and gain windward.
- moliceiro-Matriz PCI (page 3, Métodos de propulsão): The leeward toste, half-immersed and lashed to the lower mast, resists leeway; the escota adjusts sail surface and speed.
- moliceiro-Matriz PCI ([page 7]): Sailing, poling and towing from the bank are no longer the main propulsion, especially in urban canals; engines were introduced as an alternative.
practices.name: Moliceiro propulsion: poling, towing, sailing
practices.why: Moliceiro sailing in the Ria, but poling and towing are not described.

evidence: - moliceiro-Matriz PCI (A construção do Barco Moliceiro): Boat building was a knowledge passed from father to son within families, creating lineages such as Lavoura, Raimundos, Tavares, Henrique de Miranda and Garridos.
- moliceiro-Matriz PCI (A construção do Barco Moliceiro): Castro (1943) described moliceiro building as an industry existing only in this region and so traditional that its knowledge is hereditary.
- moliceiro-Matriz PCI (Os Estaleiros): Shipyards are large warehouses with earth floors, now sometimes cemented, where boats are built indoors, with a big gate for launching (the bota-abaixo).
- moliceiro-Matriz PCI (Os Estaleiros): Shipyards usually stood away from the main arms of the Ria, near streams or inside villages, often beside the builders' own homes.
- moliceiro-Matriz PCI (Os Estaleiros): Luiz de Magalhães recorded perhaps more than fifty shipyards around the Ria, mostly inland rather than near the water.
- moliceiro-Matriz PCI ([page 7]): Boatbuilding masters keep the original naval carpentry process and method for the moliceiro, with only changes in structure and size.
practices.name: Moliceiro shipyards and building knowledge
practices.why: Shipyard lineages and building knowledge are not a game activity.

evidence: - moliceiro-Matriz PCI (O processo de construção): The master begins by laying nine stakes along the boat's full length on the ground, levelled from bow to stern, spaced by the desired bottom slope.
- moliceiro-Matriz PCI (O processo de construção): Stake tops are set at different heights: first raised 0.50 m, second 0.12 m, third 0.05 m, then level, with the last raised 0.02.
practices.name: Moliceiro hull laying out on stakes
practices.why: Laying out the hull on stakes is not represented.

evidence: - moliceiro-Matriz PCI (O processo de construção): The keel board is laid first, and a line is marked across it with the pau de pontos as the master line for placing the edge boards.
- moliceiro-Matriz PCI (O processo de construção): Using the master line and pau de pontos, the builder marks the vãos and the bow and stern talões.

- moliceiro-Matriz PCI (O processo de construção): The 21 cavernas (ribs) are fitted at set spacing, alternating with caverna arms, using galvanised nails; the boat is held by props that level the bottom.
- moliceiro-Matriz PCI (O processo de construção): Caverna shape comes from moulds; each usually has three bottom holes called bueiros that let water pass inside the boat.
- moliceiro-Matriz PCI (O processo de construção): After the ribs are in place, the bow and stern posts (rodas) are fitted.

- moliceiro-Matriz PCI ([page 5]): The master boatbuilder nails the top strake (tábua de verdejar) first, fixing it through with zinc-coated nails and wooden pegs, then adds the frame arms on both sides.
practices.name: Moliceiro hull construction
practices.why: Keel and frame construction is not represented.

evidence: - moliceiro-Matriz PCI ([page 5]): The boat is caulked to seal joints and keep water out, using oakum, an iron and a caulking mallet.

- moliceiro-Matriz PCI ([page 5]): Fine pitch or pez louro is applied to the sides; black pitch goes on gunwales, bow cover, frames, traste and tostes. Rock pitch is boiled with oil in a three-legged pot.
- moliceiro-Matriz PCI ([page 5]): After the black pitch coat, sarrim is spread on top so crews do not slip while sailing; then the boat is ready for painting.
- História e Curiosidades do Bar (Barco Moliceiro - construção naval): Pine hulls were reportedly coated in black pitch to aid caulking and protect the wood from weather and water.
practices.name: Moliceiro caulking and pitching
practices.why: Caulking and pitching boats is not a game activity.

evidence: - moliceiro-Matriz PCI ([page 7]): On festival days the moliceiro was specially decorated with sails and unfurled flags, and carried wildflower branches at the bow.
practices.name: Moliceiro festival decoration
practices.why: Festival decoration with flags and branches is not offered.

evidence: - moliceiro-Matriz PCI ([page 7]): Moliço harvesting is no longer practised, but former moliceiros and ethnographic groups preserve it and regularly stage recreations of it.
practices.name: Recreations of moliço harvesting
practices.why: Seaweed gathering is playable as a museum mini-game, not as a staged heritage recreation.

evidence: - moliceiro-Matriz PCI (Transmissão): Boatbuilding skills were passed on mostly orally from master to apprentice, often father to son, in the shipyards of the Aveiro region.
- moliceiro-Matriz PCI (Transmissão): Young apprentices were first given the simple task of making wooden pegs, to see whether they had talent for the craft, before taking on bigger tasks.

- moliceiro-Matriz PCI (Transmissão): Apprentices followed masters during construction, watching and asking questions, then were gradually given tasks from simple to complex, learning through practice and experience.

- moliceiro-Matriz PCI (Transmissão): Today knowledge is still passed on mainly in shipyards, but demand to learn the craft is very low; occasional vocational courses connect masters with young people.

- moliceiro-Matriz PCI (Transmissão): Building and painting techniques have been recorded in books, in licensing and approval project documents detailing construction features, and in videos and documentaries with masters and painters.
- moliceiro-Matriz PCI (Part 10, end of builders section): Five master builders currently work regularly: three with yards in Pardilhó and two in Torreira.
practices.name: Moliceiro boatbuilding knowledge transmission
practices.why: Oral transmission of boatbuilding skills is not represented.

evidence: - História e Curiosidades do Bar (A Origem): Farmers adapted tools such as rakes for harvesting moliço, and modified fishing and transport boats to ease loading it.
practices.name: Adaptation of tools and boats for moliço harvesting
practices.why: Adapting tools and boats for loading moliço is not modelled.
